candidates.speaker: Eric Hernandez
candidates.proposition: Naturalism loses simplicity and explanatory power when it adds irreducible moral and conscious properties instead of reducing them to the physical.
candidates.attributionBasis: The alternating dialogue and the speaker's favorable comparison of theism against naturalist accounts identify Hernandez as the source.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly challenges naturalism's advertised explanatory economy and argues that its accommodations of consciousness and morality weaken its comparative case.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Schieber's claim that consciousness may be an irreducible intrinsic aspect of fundamentally physical reality.

candidates.contextSummary: After Schieber describes science as silent about intrinsic nature, Hernandez argues that multiplying irreducible nonphysical features makes naturalism increasingly selective and costly.

candidates.speaker: Justin Schieber
candidates.proposition: Accepting irreducible consciousness is a motivated inference from consciousness and the limits of physics, rather than an ad hoc rescue of naturalism.
candidates.attributionBasis: The first-person defense of the naturalist consciousness view directly answers Hernandez's accusation and matches Schieber's preceding position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This reply protects naturalism from a major simplicity objection by explaining why its additional intrinsic properties are evidentially motivated despite their strangeness.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hernandez's charge that irreducible conscious properties make naturalism ad hoc and reduce its simplicity and explanatory power.

candidates.contextSummary: Schieber concedes some loss of simplicity but argues that undeniable consciousness, its irreducibility, and physics' epistemic limits jointly motivate his monist account.

candidates.speaker: Justin Schieber
candidates.proposition: Grounding moral value in God's nature remains metaethical subjectivism because God is a person and therefore a subject.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly characterizes Eric's view from the opposing position and develops Schieber's person-based subjectivism objection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move contests a principal theistic argument by denying that divine grounding supplies the objective morality Hernandez claims theism uniquely explains.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hernandez's opening claim that objective moral value is grounded in God as the ultimate moral standard.

candidates.contextSummary: When the discussion turns to evil and morality, Schieber argues that dependence on the nature of any person, including God, is dependence on a subject.

candidates.speaker: Eric Hernandez
candidates.proposition: Objective morality is standardly understood as truth independent of human thought, so divine grounding is compatible with moral objectivity under a common definition.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker quotes a moral realist definition to defend Eric's stated terminology and directly answers Schieber's characterization of it as nonstandard.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This definitional defense is necessary for Hernandez's moral argument because it preserves the claim that God can ground morality without making it human-subjective.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Schieber's contention that Hernandez uses objective morality nonstandardly and that grounding value in a divine person is subjectivist.

candidates.contextSummary: Hernandez appeals to a secular moral philosopher's formulation and contrasts objective truths independent of human opinion with morality dependent on human judgment.

candidates.speaker: Justin Schieber
candidates.proposition: A deeper form of objectivity must be independent of every particular person, so morality grounded in God's nature cannot be ultimately objective.
candidates.attributionBasis: The response distinguishes a human-independent definition from person-independent objectivity and concludes against theistic metaethical grounding.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The distinction prevents the definitional reply from resolving the dispute and sharpens the con case that divine moral grounding retains an arbitrary personal basis.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hernandez's cited definition of objective morality as moral truth independent specifically of human thought and opinion.

candidates.contextSummary: Schieber grants that one usage may exclude only human opinion but argues that substantive ultimate objectivity cannot rely on any person's nature, including God's.

candidates.speaker: Eric Hernandez
candidates.proposition: Necessary, eternal, personal moral properties are best grounded in a necessary, eternal, personal transcendent being rather than in finite subjects or abstractions.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly advances grounding in God and contrasts God with a finite person while answering the charge of arbitrariness.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the positive grounding inference at the heart of the pro moral argument, connecting the alleged features of morality to the attributes of God.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Schieber's objection that calling a God-grounded moral standard objective is arbitrary, ad hoc, and dependent on a subject.

candidates.contextSummary: Hernandez argues that morality's necessity, eternality, and personal or obligation-conferring character point toward a transcendent personal ground rather than a finite individual.

candidates.speaker: Justin Schieber
candidates.proposition: Evolutionary animal suffering is especially evidential because predatory body plans appear properly directed toward tearing apart and consuming other animals.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly recalls his opening argument about evolutionary suffering, which is the con argument attributed to Schieber in the surrounding exchange.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move states a principal evidential argument from animal suffering against theism, focusing on apparently designed predatory functions rather than generic evil.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hernandez's use of teleology and evil in support of theism and the moderator's request to examine his argument from suffering.

candidates.contextSummary: Returning to the argument from evil, Schieber emphasizes that many animals function normally precisely when their evolved anatomy inflicts severe suffering on prey.

candidates.speaker: Eric Hernandez
candidates.proposition: Animal suffering can be attributed to humanity's fall, which affected all creation and deviated nature from its intended teleology, potentially even from the beginning.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explains the Christian fall, humanity's disobedience, and altered creation as a defense of Hernandez's theistic position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the principal theistic explanation offered in the exchange for predation and animal suffering, directly addressing a major component of the con case.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Schieber's evolutionary argument that predatory animal structures and suffering appear teleologically normal and count against theism.

candidates.contextSummary: Hernandez says human disobedience affected animals, plants, and the wider creation, and suggests divine foreknowledge could permit fallen conditions throughout natural history.

candidates.speaker: Justin Schieber
candidates.proposition: The fall explanation lacks a specified mechanism and fine-grained predictive power connecting human sin to predatory anatomy and non-vegetarian ecosystems.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker presses Eric directly for predictions and a mechanism, consistently expressing Schieber's critique of the proposed fall explanation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection attacks the explanatory adequacy of the pro theodicy by arguing that it accommodates observed suffering retrospectively without predicting its specific forms.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hernandez's proposal that humanity's fall altered all creation and can explain animal predation even across earlier natural history.

candidates.contextSummary: Schieber asks what conditions would precede the fall and how sin could transform peaceful creatures into animals anatomically equipped to tear one another apart.

candidates.speaker: Justin Schieber
candidates.proposition: A successful theodicy must be more probable than its negation given theism and must jointly with theism explain the specific evil under dispute.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker formulates explicit adequacy conditions for a theodicy and says Eric has supplied too little detail to assess, identifying Schieber's critical role.
candidates.loadBearingReason: These criteria establish the evaluative burden for the fall defense and explain why merely predicting unspecified bad consequences does not answer the evidential argument.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hernandez's broad claim that departing from God's plan predictably produces horrible consequences and thereby accounts for worldly suffering.

candidates.contextSummary: Schieber formalizes his challenge by requiring both antecedent plausibility and explanatory fit, then argues that Hernandez's fall account lacks enough substance for either assessment.
